briefing.opening: Good morning. I will now begin the climate change expert spokesperson briefing for August 4, 2026.

sections.title: 🔴 Extreme Weather Events and Severe Damages
sections.content: Today's briefing begins with news of intensifying extreme weather events and their severe consequences worldwide. In Korea, a 122-year record heatwave and the worst drought are materializing as a 'climate disaster.' In Jeonju, a 'severe heatwave warning' was issued for the first time in the province, increasing the estimated number of heat-related deaths in the Jeonbuk region alone to five [17, 90, 91]. This heatwave highlighted the issue of cooling blind spots in traditional markets, leading to operational suspensions, and even threatening the survival of urban green space trees in Buk-gu, Ulsan [2, 19, 23]. Europe also faces a severe situation with 20,000 deaths due to unprecedented extreme heat and the drying up of the Danube River. In Hungary, the risk of nuclear power plant shutdowns due to drought was even mentioned [3, 92, 105, 107]. The unpredictable repercussions of climate change are exacerbating agricultural production instability and posing a global health warning, underscoring the urgent need for comprehensive preparedness against climate disasters [4, 9, 97].

sections.title: ⚠️ Multifaceted Impacts of Climate Change and Social Vulnerability
sections.content: Beyond extreme weather, climate change is exerting multifaceted impacts across society, revealing vulnerabilities. The degree to which the severity of the climate crisis is perceived and negative reactions are expressed is higher among women, raising the need for gender-sensitive climate adaptation measures [1]. In Hallasan and Jeju regions, 'early warning' signals of climate change have been detected, such as bats waking up and foraging even in mid-winter, indicating the seriousness of ecosystem changes [12, 15, 16]. Furthermore, developing countries face vulnerability to price and productivity changes and climate change, with research suggesting that the malaria map in Africa will be redrawn due to climate change [8, 95, 100, 102]. As climate change causes instability in agricultural production and affects environmental diseases like allergies both domestically and internationally, systematic management and adaptation efforts are crucial [9, 22, 25].

sections.title: 🌱 Domestic and International Efforts and Citizen Participation Towards Carbon Neutrality
sections.content: On a positive note, various domestic and international efforts and citizen participation towards carbon neutrality are expanding. In Korea, corporate sustainability reports continue, with Samsung Securities establishing a climate change response system and GS Caltex obtaining greenhouse gas reduction and recycling certifications [10, 14]. Local governments and educational institutions are also actively participating, encouraging citizen action, such as Gwangmyeong City's 'Climate Volunteers' surpassing 20,000 members and the Nonsan-Gyeryong Office of Education using reusable aprons [39, 40, 42, 47]. Additionally, Jeju National University and Korea Midland Power signed an MOU to achieve carbon neutrality in Jeju, and in the National Assembly, Representative Park Jie-won is directly practicing carbon neutrality by introducing hydrogen cars as official vehicles [38, 41, 43, 45, 46, 48, 49, 52]. In this way, government, corporations, and civil society are collectively exploring various measures to achieve carbon neutrality, responding to the 'era of net-zero competition' [37].

sections.title: 🇰🇷 Accelerating Renewable Energy Transition and Policy Challenges
sections.content: Finally, let's examine the acceleration of renewable energy transition and related policy challenges. The Ministry of Climate has declared an 'Electric Nation' with the goal of achieving 100GW of renewable energy early, promoting innovation in water supply in line with the AI era [53, 58, 60, 67]. The President emphasized the inevitability of a renewable energy-centric transition, proposing the prevention of regional decline through solar farming, and the government is expanding policy support, including promoting the introduction of renewable energy tax credits [57, 72]. However, concerns are raised that delays in renewable energy deployment could hinder the achievement of the 2035 greenhouse gas reduction target, along with criticism that Korea is 10 years behind in the solar revolution [71, 87, 93, 69, 85]. In the agriculture and rural sectors, a win-win model is being pursued to increase farm household income and repair agricultural infrastructure through the expansion of floating solar power, but controversies over solar project methods and the need for agricultural financial support are also being discussed [62, 76, 77, 79, 81, 82]. Internationally, market changes are active, with Germany announcing a complete overhaul of renewable energy subsidies in 2026, and UK's Shell selling its European onshore renewable energy business to France's TotalEnergies [56, 63, 74, 86, 88].

briefing.closing: As we have seen in today's briefing, climate change is a global threat, yet innovative efforts and policy shifts to overcome it are simultaneously underway. We must continue to build a better future through sustained interest and participation. This concludes today's climate briefing.
